comments.content: The validation now accepts every `SettingScope` value, but `SettingScope` also contains `System` and `SystemDefaults` (settings.ts), which `disableExtension` explicitly rejects. Since the old `choices: [User, Workspace]` restriction was removed, `--scope system` now passes validation and is silently treated as `User` by `handleDisable`, so the command reports success while disabling at the wrong scope. Restrict the accepted values to the scopes this command actually supports, and compute the normalized list once instead of repeating the `.map(...).toLowerCase()` expression.

`handleDisable` is exported and silently maps any value other than "workspace" (including typos or unsupported scopes like "system") to `SettingScope.User`, so an invalid scope disables the extension in the wrong place without any error. Prefer resolving the scope explicitly and throwing on unknown values. Note this if/else is a verbatim copy of `handleEnable` in enable.ts plus the duplicated validation block in both `builder`s — consider extracting a shared `parseScope()`/`validateScope()` helper to keep the two commands in sync.

The validation now accepts every value of `SettingScope`, including `system` and `systemdefaults`, whereas the previous `choices: [SettingScope.User, SettingScope.Workspace]` rejected them. Since `handleEnable` silently maps any non-workspace scope to `SettingScope.User`, running `enable --scope system foo` will now succeed and enable the extension at user scope instead of reporting an error. Restrict the allowed values to `User`/`Workspace` (validation should not be broader than what the handler supports).

Normalization is asymmetric: `fromInput` runs `ensureLeadingAndTrailingSlash` (adds leading/trailing `/`, converts `\` → `/`), but `fromFileRule` does not. `isEnabled` now tests rules against a normalized path (`ensureLeadingAndTrailingSlash(currentPath)`), so rules already persisted by the previous implementation stop matching:
- Legacy non-glob rules (e.g. `/home/user`, written when `includeSubdirs` was false) compile to `^/home/user$` and no longer match `/home/user/`.
- Rules written on Windows (e.g. `C:\Users\foo*`) keep backslashes, while the tested path is normalized to `/C:/Users/foo/...`, so they never match.
Result: a user's `!` disable rule is silently ignored after upgrade and the extension becomes enabled in a path they explicitly disabled. The same asymmetry also makes `isEqualTo`/`conflictsWith`/`isChildOf` miss legacy equivalents, so `enable()` appends a normalized rule next to the stale one and duplicates accumulate.

Suggest normalizing `baseRule` here as well (guard the empty string so a bare `*` keeps its match-everything meaning).
